Human kinome screen. All drug treatment, washing, fixing and Hoechst staining steps were performed using the SAMI-integrated automated screening system (Beckman Coulter). HeLa/TFEB-GFP were seeded at a density of 7,000 cells per well in 96-well plates using a Multidrop and incubated at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO incubator for 12 hours prior to treatment. On each plate, four wells were seeded with parental HeLa cells for imaging background controls, eight wells of cells were treated with 0.1% DMSO as drug vehicle controls, and four wells of cells were treated with 250 nM Torin1 as nuclear translocation positive controls. For the remaining wells, each well was treated with one of the 436 drugs within the L1200 library from SelleckChem. Each drug was applied under five different conditions: 10 μM for 6 hours, 3 μM for 6 hours, 1 μM for 6 hours, 10 μM for 1 hour, and 3 μM for 1 hour. After treatment, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 20 minutes and incubated with 2 μM Hoechst 33342 overnight at 4°C. The cells were washed with PBS, and the plates were sealed. Imaging was performed using the IN Cell 2000 Analyzer (GE Healthcare Life Sciences) with FITC (for TFEB-GFP) and DAPI (for nuclei) channels at 20X magnification. Sixteen fields were captured for each well. The acquired images were analyzed with the IN Cell 1000 Workstation analyzer software. DAPI channel images were used to segment the nuclei and identify individual cells for TFEB-GFP intensity measurements. Intensity analysis was conducted by measuring the average intensity of the whole cell. Drugs that yielded intensities greater than the average intensity for all 436 drugs plus four times the standard deviation were considered as outliers and were excluded from further analysis. The Multi Target Analysis Module was used to measure the average nuclear intensity (N) and the average intensity within a 2 µm collar (C) surrounding the nucleus, as the cytoplasmic sampling region.

Kinome Data analysis. TFEB nuclear translocation index (NT index) was calculated as N/(N+C), which ranges from 0 to 1, and was divided into 100 equal intervals. The frequencies of cells falling into each interval were calculated, resulting in 100 data points for each drug, which constitute the distribution curve for each drug and are referred to as the frequency data points. To assess the similarity of the 436 distribution curves to the control distribution curves of DMSO and Torin1, a heatmap was generated using python. The similarity was quantified using the formula: D * D , where D represents the DMSO Torin1 DMSO similarity to the DMSO control curves and DTorin1 represents the similarity to the Torin1 control curves. In addition, intensity analysis was conducted by measuring the average intensity of the whole cell. To cluster components based on the frequency data points, several steps were taken to ensure proper normalization and clustering. Initially, min-max normalization was applied to each drug's frequency data points. This step scaled the values to the range of 0 to 1. Subsequently, we applied quantile normalization to the control components' data (DMSO and Torin1), which rescaled the frequency data points to a unified scale among all controls and mitigated variations in measurement scales. Following this, frequency data points of all other drugs were adjusted. This adjustment was performed based on the average impact of the quantile normalization on the control data for the associated plates. We then combined the data from different conditions into a single data table for ease of analysis.

To identify the relationships between drugs, we computed cosine similarities (distances). These values were utilized in hierarchical clustering, where we implemented single-linkage clustering. In this methodology, the distance between clusters is defined as the shortest distance between any two points in the clusters. In the resulting matrix, each entry signifies the correlation value between the adjusted frequency data points of the two corresponding drugs. Moreover, we calculated the distances between each drug and the mean frequency data points of corresponding Torin1 and DMSO values. These distances were computed using the correlation values that were previously calculated for each drug in relation to all other drugs.

Following completion of the treatment, cells were washed once with cold PBS and lysed using either NP-40 lysis buffer (150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 50 mM Tris-Cl pH 8.0) or RIPA buffer (150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton-X100, 50 mM Tris-Cl pH 8.0, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate and 0.1% SDS) supplemented with 1X protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The total lysates were kept at 4°C with agitation for 1 hour, followed by centrifugation at 16,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C to remove debris. The protein concentration was measured using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Cat# 23225, Thermo Scientific), with Pierce™ Bovine Serum Albumin Standard, 2 mg/mL (Cat# 23210, Thermo Scientific) as the standard. Protein samples were prepared by adding Laemmli sample buffer (Cat# 1610737EDU, biorad) and incubating at 95°C for 5 minutes. The samples were then stored at −80°C until use. Denatured samples were separated by SDS-PAGE and subsequently transferred onto PVDF membranes (Cat# 1620177, Biorad). The membranes were incubated in blocking buffer (5%, w/v, dried skimmed milk in Tris-buffered saline, pH 7.4, and 0.1% Tween 20, TBST), followed by overnight incubation with the indicated primary antibodies, appropriately diluted in the blocking buffer. Subsequently, the membranes were washed three times with TBST and incubated with the appropriate secondary antibodies, either Goat anti-mouse HRP-conjugated antibody (Cat# 1705047, Biorad) or Goat anti-rabbit HRP-conjugated antibody (Cat# 1705046, Biorad) or IRDye® 680RD Goat anti-Mouse IgG Secondary Antibody (926-68070, 1:10000, LI-COR Biosciences) or IRDye® 800CW Goat anti- Rabbit IgG Secondary Antibody (926-32211, 1:10000, LI-COR Biosciences), diluted in blocking buffer, for 1 h at room temperature. After washing, the membranes were detected using SuperSignal™ West Dura Extended Duration Substrate reagent (Cat# A38554, ThermoFisher Scientific). Images were taken with ImageQuant LAS 4000 (GE Healthcare) and quantified by Fiji analysis software. Uncropped scans of all blots are provided in Source data file.

Immunoprecipitation. Protein extraction from cultured HEK293T and HeLa cells was performed with either RIPA buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% NP-40, 0.1% SDS) or NP-40 lysis buffer. Centrifugation was performed at 16,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C to remove cell debris. For lysates in RIPA buffer, the volume of the lysate was roughly measured, and powdered SDS was added in proportion to the volume to achieve a final concentration of 1% SDS. The lysate was then boiled at 95°C for 5 minutes to dissociate any non-covalently bound proteins. Subsequently, RIPA buffer without SDS was added to reduce the SDS concentration back to 0.1%. The lysates were then pre-cleared using dynabeads (Cat# 10003D, Invitrogen) conjugated with normal mouse IgG (Cat# 12-371, Sigma Aldrich). The pre-cleared lysates were then incubated with dynabeads conjugated to the indicated primary antibodies, rotating at 4°C for 2 hours. Subsequently, the beads were washed four times with 500 μL of RIPA lysis buffer and eluted in 2x Laemmli buffer at 95°C for 5 minutes.

The dephosphorylation master mix is composed of 1x λ Protein Phosphatase Buffer (Cat# L9288), 1x MnCl2 (Cat# M0564), 1x protease inhibitor (Cat# P3100-010) and about 16 units per μl λ phosphatase. Sample preparation and LC-MS analysis for phosphorylation detection.
For phosphorylated TFEB from the in vitro IKK kinase phosphorylation: Phosphorylated TFEB protein was prepared as described in the “in vitro kinase assay” section. Three aliquots of in vitro phosphorylated TFEB was used as n=3 replicates for this analysis. To remove MS-incompatible reagents, TFEB was isolated by acetone precipitation. Dry TFEB was reconstituted in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate buffer, pH 7, reduced using dithiothreitol (Cat#20291, Pierce), alkylated using iodoacetamide (Cat#A3221, Sigma-Alrich), and digested using sequencing grade trypsin (Cat#V5113, Promega). TFEB tryptic peptides were dried and reconstituted in LC-MS mobile phase A (2% acetonitrile (Cat# 047138.M6, Thermo Scientific), 98% MilliQ purified water, 0.1% formic acid (Cat# 85178, Pierce)) for LC-MS analysis. We used a Thermo Fisher Ultimate RSLC3000 nanoLC system equipped with a micro silica column packed with 20 cm of ReproSil-Pur C18 resin (120Å, C18-AQ,1.9-μmresin; Cat# r119.aq, Dr. Maisch) and an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid Mass Spectrometer. Our acquisition method includes an untargeted acquisition in parallel with a targeted acquisition for the tryptic phosphopeptides 406AA-430AA and 406AA-431AA. This approach allows a general analysis of TFEB tryptic peptides and targeted analysis of select candidate phosphopeptides for further fragmentation that ultimately enables the rigorous localization of the phosphorylation sites. The untargeted acquisition settings include Orbitrap as the detector, top 15 data dependent MS2, charge state selection 2-6, 60K and 30K was set as the Orbitrap resolution for MS1 and MS2 respectively, 250-2000 m/z scan range, 30% RF lens, 0.8 m/z isolation window, stepped HCD at 28%, 30%, 34% collision energy for fragmentation, and profile as acquired data type. The targeted acquisition involves MS2 acquisition, and the settings include a targeted precursor list of m/z 881.73 and m/z 924.43, Orbitrap as the detector, 30K Orbitrap resolution, scan range is 110-2000 m/z, 30% RF lens, stepped HCD fragmentation with 28%, 30%, and 32% collision energy. These fragmentation parameters are optimized to minimize the loss of phosphate for the targeted phosphopeptides. We used our in-house software (TDMS 7.04) to process the LC-MS data using UniProt database P19484 for TFEB122, 123. The data shows a clear presence of the intact phosphorylated peptide at 406AA-430AA with m/z 881.7311 (-1.99 ppm error, expected mass of 881.732851 m/z). The subsequent MS2 data exhibits multiple ion types supporting phosphorylation localization at S427. We also manually validated the MS2 fragment ions independently using Qualbrowser (Thermo Scientific Excalibur 4.3) to ensure confident phosphorylation site localization. No statistical tests were applied to the mass spectrometry data, as phosphorylation site localization was determined based on qualitative MS2 fragment ion evidence.

Unreacted iodoacetamide was washed away from the filter with two sequential additions of 200 µl UA buffer and centrifugation at 14,000 x g for 15 to 20 minutes after each addition. The top filter units were transferred to a new collection tube and 0.2 µg of Asp-N (Cat# 9053, Pierce) was added and samples were digested at 37 °C overnight. The next day, 0.1 µg of sequencing-grade trypsin (Cat# V5113, Promega) was added and samples were digested for two hours at 37 °C. The filters were spun at 14,000 x g for 15 minutes to collect the peptides in the flow through. The filter was washed with 50 µl of 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate buffer and the wash was collected with the peptides. (C4, BIOMEKNT3C04, and C18, BIOMEKNT3C18) (Glygen) on a Beckman robot (Biomek NX), as previously described125. An aliquot (10%) was removed for quantification using the Pierce Quantitative Fluorometric Peptide Assay kit (Cat# 23290, Thermo Scientific). The peptides were analyzed using a nano-Elute chromatograph (Bruker Daltonics) coupled online to a hybrid trapped ion mobility-quadrupole time of flight mass spectrometer (timsTOF Pro2, Bruker Daltonics with a modified nano-electrospray source (CaptiveSpray, Bruker Daltonics). ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Xiong et al. investigated the mechanisms regulating TFEB protein turnover. By performing a human kinome screening, the authors found that IKK inhibition strongly stabilized TFEB and promoted its nuclear translocation. They also found that silencing of IKK subunits resulted in increased TFEB protein levels. IKK was able to phosphorylate TFEB in vitro at multiple serine residues. The authors propose that multisite TFEB phosphorylation by IKK primes TFEB for  -TrCP2-mediated ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Although results of this work may be interesting in principle, there are several issues that require further clarification. First, the physiological relevance of IKK-mediated degradation of TFEB is unclear. The authors propose that IKK regulates basal TFEB protein turnover. However, the IKK complex is mainly inactive under basal conditions and its activity is well-known to be induced by a plethora of stimuli, including inflammatory inputs (e.g. cytokines, PAMPs, etc). It is therefore quite puzzling that TFEB stability is controlled by an inactive kinase. In addition, how the IKK complex is involved in the degradation of TFEB upon IKK-activating stimuli has not been properly addressed. Furthermore, the authors show that IKK inhibition results not only in increased stability but also in TFEB nuclear translocation. However, the relationship between these two processes has not been investigated in detail. Finally, there are major issues with the interpretation of some of the data, as listed below. Specific points: 1. As stated above, the physiological relevance for the role of IKK in TFEB degradation is unclear. The authors propose that the IKK/ -TrCP2 axis regulates basal TFEB protein turnover. For instance, on page 12 the authors state that “ -TrCP2 functions as a default TFEB ubiquitin ligase”. However, the IKK complex is mainly inactive under basal conditions and its activity is well-known to be induced by several stimuli, including inflammatory inputs (e.g. cytokines, PAMPs, etc). How can basal TFEB stability be controlled by an inactive kinase? For instance, IKKbeta- and IKKgamma-KO cells are characterized by impaired degradation of its main substrate IkBalpha in response to IKK-activating stimuli, such as TNFalpha, whereas basal IkBalpha levels are unaffected in IKK-KO cells. The authors should check basal IkBalpha levels in their IKK-silenced cells. Also, the use of IKKbeta- and IKKgamma-KO cells is needed in order to check basal TFEB (and IkBalpha) levels in a more relevant cellular system. 2. Related to the previous point, the role of IKK-mediated TFEB degradation has not been properly addressed in physiologically relevant conditions. For instance, despite being a well-known IKK-activating stimulus, TNFalpha does not seem to induce a significant TFEB degradation (Figure 3e), as opposite to LPS stimulation which promotes a strong reduction in TFEB levels (Figure 3f). This is in contrast with a role of IKK as a key mediator of TFEB degradation. Do other well-known IKK-activating stimuli, such as IL-1, promote TFEB degradation? Furthermore, to define whether IKK is indeed a physiological mediator of TFEB phosphorylation/degradation, the authors should assess whether the levels of TFEB are affected in IKKbeta- and IKKgamma-KO cells in response to LPS, TFNalpha and IL-1 stimulation, as compared to WT-stimulated cells. 3. What is the relationship between IKK-mediated TFEB phosphorylation and nuclear translocation? The authors show that the IKK-16 inhibitor stabilized TFEB levels but also strongly promoted its nuclear translocation (Figure 1c). Does IKK silencing also promote TFEB nuclear translocation? Also, what is the subcellular localization of TFEB in IKK-KO cells? The authors showed that the use of IKK-16 also results in mTORC1 inhibition (Supplementary Figure 2a, b), but stated that “the two processes are uncoupled”. In order to determine whether the effect of IKK-16 on TFEB stabilization is uncoupled from mTORC1 inhibition, the authors should use this inhibitor in cells with constitutive mTORC1 activity (i.e. cells expressing constitutively active Rag GTPases) and assess TFEB levels and subcellular localization. 4. I have major issues with the interpretation of some results. The authors state that, opposite to WT TFEB, the levels of TFEB-6xA remained stable upon cycloheximide or LPS treatment (Figures 3d and 3f). However, the starting levels of TFEB-6xA are much higher compared to WT-TFEB, which makes very difficult any comparison between the two constructs. Despite this, I do see a clear decrease in TFEB-6xA levels upon these treatments (Figures 3d and 3f), thus arguing against the conclusions made by the authors. Similar issues apply to Figure 5e, when comparing the levels of WT-TFEB to TFEB-6xA upon  -TrCP2 silencing, and to Figure 6i, when using the TFEB-KKRR mutant. The authors should use similar starting protein levels and a similar exposure to make any comparisons between the two plasmids. 5. It is quite puzzling that, when performing transient transfections, no differences are observed in the levels of wt, 6xA-, and KKRR-TFEB (Supplementary Figure 7a, b). The authors state that this puzzling difference, compared to the stable cell lines, occurs “presumably because the very high protein levels associated with transient transfection by themselves overwhelm the processing abilities of IKK/b-TrCP2…”. It is surprising that the authors did not test this hypothesis, as it could be easily tested by transfecting lower amounts of wt and mutant TFEB. When doing so, is the stability of transiently transfected TFEB mutants affected? Do they show a different degradation pattern in response to LPS or TNFalpha stimulation? 6. The authors should generate and use a 6xD/6xE TFEB phospho-mimetic mutant. Does IKK-16 or IKK depletion stabilize this construct? 7. The rationale for focusing on  -TrCP2 as a putative TFEB ubiquitin ligase is unclear. In Figure 4a, DCAF7 appears to have a strong effect on TFEB ubiquitination. Yet, the authors only focused on  -TrCP2. What is the effect of DCAF7 depletion on TFEB stability? What is the effect of either DCAF7 or  -TrCP2 depletion on LPS-mediated TFEB degradation? 8. I found surprising that the authors only assessed the levels of the TFEB-KKRR mutant in response to  -TrCP2 silencing. It is indeed crucial to test the effect of  -TrCP2 or DCAF7 overexpression on TFEB-KKRR protein levels and ubiquitination. Furthermore, the effect of both IKK-16 and IKKbeta and IKKgamma depletion on this mutant should also be assessed. 9. The authors state that Torin1 did not influence TFEB stability. However, previous evidence showed the opposite (PMID: 27268034). In addition, the authors found that rapalogs induce TFEB nuclear translocation. However, TFEB is a well-known rapamycin-insensitive mTORC1 substrate (PMID: 22692423, 22343943, 21617040). How do the authors explain the discrepancy of their findings with previous work? These data raise serious concerns on the cellular systems and/or methods that the authors used to assess TFEB localization and stability. 10. TFEB ubiquitination experiments need to be performed at higher standards. To avoid the presence of confounding contaminants and properly assess TFEB ubiquitination, extracts need to be boiled in 1% SDS prior immunoprecipitation, which ensures the dissociation of any non-covalently bound proteins. Please see PMID: 17991829 (or many other references on the topic) for a more detailed protocol. 11. Detailed information on the protocol used for the kinase assays should be provided in the methods section.

### Reviewer 2

To authors The authors report a potential regulation of the lysosomal activity and autophagy-controlling transcription factor TFEB by the IκB kinase (IKK)-proteasome pathway, which results in subsequent phosphorylation, βTrCP2-mediated ubiquitination and proteolytic degradation of TFEB following cellular stimulation. Serine cluster and potential ubiquitination sites were identified using tagged transfected components. These degron residues can be removed without affecting the transcriptional activity or nuclear translocation of TFEB. The analyses were almost exclusively performed in in vitro systems and/or by using transfected molecules. Technical or conceptional flaws are seen in several experiments. The potential biological significance remains unclear: Why should all physiological NF-κB-activating stimuli, which result in IKK activation, cause a degradation of TFEB? No physiological evidence is provided to support a hypothesis for IKK to TFEB signaling. Only HeLa and 293T cells have been used. The authors should have included non-cancerous/transformed cell types and analysis of the endogenous proteins and multiple IKK stimuli and provide genetic evidence (e.g. mouse models) for their hypothesis. The analysis of the degron and ubiquitination does not provide significant advance over the analysis of other already known IKK substrates. The paper does not provide sufficient advance to be considered for Nature Communications. Some specific points: Fig. 1b. This is a debatable strategy to use kinase inhibitors because perhaps none of these inhibitors is selective for the presumed target kinase and IKK requires cellular stimulation with specific agents to be activated. In non-stimulated cells IKK has very low basal activity. Why then should an IKK inhibitor be effective on TFEB-GFP in this experiment? As said, the inhibitor IKK-16 is not selective and also inhibits LRRK2. How can indirect effects of the drugs on cell viability, affecting apparent TFEB levels, and on cell cycle be controlled? Fig. 2c. The effect of IKK-16 on TFEB nuclear translocation should be confirmed by using a additional, different IKK inhibitor and/or siRNA-mediated silencing of IKKβ or γ. Fig. 1e. Why are there two main bands for each, IKKα and IKKβ and also for IKKγ? Both bands for α and β (and γ) are affected by the respective siRNA, but the migration of at least one them does not fit to the known molecular weight. It is completely unexpected, and contradicts comprehensive literature knowledge, that siIKBKG strongly affects IKKα protein level. Why should this be? The effect of siRNAs on endogenous TFEB is not convincing. Fig. 2. Recombinant TFEB-3xFlag was expressed in HeLa cells, isolated, dephosphorylated by λ-phosphatase, phosphorylated in vitro by purified IKKβ (or IKKα). This approach likely results in artificial substrate phosphorylation events, which are meaningless in intact cells. Furthermore, substrate recognition in intact cells may involve association of IKKβ with NEMO/IKKγ. The problem of their approach is consistent when comparing the sites with intact cell-derived data in PhosphoSitePlus: Ser401 and 427 are not indicated as phosphorylated human TFEB. A determination of phosphorylation sites by mass spectrometry on endogenous TFEB after stimulation with IKK-activating agents is required. Fig. 3. The rapid and almost complete degradation of transfected tagged TFEB by LPS and much weaker or even marginally so by TNFα (panels e and f) is surprising since IKK is activated more strongly by TNFα, as many studies have shown. The IκB control is missing in panel f. The tag may interfere with degradation. It is important that degradation of endogenous TFEB is shown. Fig. 3d. That TFEB-6xA is stabilized in CHX treated cells rather suggest that kinases other than IKK phosphorylate these residues in the “WT” version, since IKK is not active in non-stimulated cells. Fig. 4 and S6. In some cases, proteasomal inhibition is needed to show elevated HA-ubiquitinated species, in others not.
